title: What the Operating System Does for a Program
summary: Between your program and the hardware sits the **operating system**. It loads the program into memory, gives it a private **address space**, shares the CPU between hundreds of programs, and is the only way to reach files, the screen or the network. Each of these ideas gets its own chapter later; this lesson is the map.
markdown:
## The program is not alone On the tiny computer from lesson 1.01, one program owned the whole machine. A Windows PC runs hundreds of programs at once: the game, the browser, the music player, dozens of background services. None of them can be allowed to overwrite another's memory or hog the processor forever. The **operating system** (OS) is the program that makes sharing possible. Its core, the **kernel**, runs with full control of the hardware. Everything else, including your game, runs with restricted rights and has to ask the kernel for anything that touches the outside world. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph USER["User mode: restricted"] G["Your game"] B["Browser"] M["Music player"] end subgraph KERNEL["Kernel mode: full control"] K["Windows kernel
memory, scheduling, security"] D["Drivers
disk, graphics, input"] end G --> K B --> K M --> K K --> D D --> HW["Hardware"] ``` Chapter 15 looks inside the kernel. For now, five jobs matter. ## 1. Loading the program An `.exe` on disk is a file in the **PE format** (Portable Executable). When you start it, the Windows **loader**: 1. Creates a new **process**: the container for one running copy of a program. 2. Maps the `.exe` file's code and data into the process's memory. 3. Loads every **DLL** the program needs (such as `kernel32.dll` and the C++ runtime), and fills in the addresses of the functions the program calls in them. 4. Creates the first **thread** and starts it at the program's entry point, which eventually calls your `main`. Chapter 9 takes the PE format apart byte by byte. Chapter 4 builds DLLs of your own. ## 2. Giving each process its own memory Every process gets its own **virtual address space**. The addresses your program prints are not positions in the RAM chips. They are positions in a private, pretend memory that the OS and the processor translate to real memory behind the scenes. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph A["Game's addresses"] A1["0x7FF6...1000"] end subgraph B["Browser's addresses"] B1["0x7FF6...1000"] end A1 --> R1["RAM page 51,203"] B1 --> R2["RAM page 9,876"] ``` Two programs can both use the address `0x7FF61000`, and they reach different physical memory. That is how Windows keeps programs from reading or wrecking each other: there is simply no address in one process that leads to another process's memory. Memory is handed out in **pages**, which are 4,096 bytes (`0x1000`) each on x64. Chapter 6 explains the translation and how to explore your own address space. ## 3. Sharing the processor A CPU has a handful of cores, and there are thousands of threads that want to run. The OS **scheduler** gives each thread a short turn, a **time slice** of a few milliseconds, then saves its registers and lets another thread run. It switches so often that everything appears to run at once. This is why your game's frame time is never perfectly steady, and why one program stuck in an endless loop does not freeze the whole PC. Chapter 6 covers threads and scheduling. ## 4. Being the only door to the hardware User-mode programs cannot touch the disk, the graphics card or the network directly. They call **system calls**, functions that switch the CPU into kernel mode, do the work with full rights and switch back. On Windows you almost never make system calls yourself. You call documented functions in DLLs, the **Windows API**, and those make the system calls for you. ```cpp #include #include int main() { SYSTEM_INFO info{}; GetSystemInfo(&info); // asks Windows about the machine and the address space std::cout << "Page size: " << info.dwPageSize << " bytes\n"; std::cout << "Allocation granularity: " << info.dwAllocationGranularity << " bytes\n"; std::cout << "Lowest usable address: " << info.lpMinimumApplicationAddress << '\n'; return 0; } ``` ``` Page size: 4096 bytes Allocation granularity: 65536 bytes Lowest usable address: 0000000000010000 ``` `GetSystemInfo` is part of the Windows API, declared in `` and implemented in `kernel32.dll`. Chapter 5 is all about this API: how to read its documentation, handle its errors and use its strange string types. Even `std::cout` ends in a system call. The C++ library collects your text, then calls `WriteFile` in `kernel32.dll`, which asks the kernel to put the bytes on the console. ## 5. Keeping track of who owns what When your program opens a file, the kernel creates an object to represent the open file and hands your process a **handle**: a small number that means "that file I opened". Threads, processes, events and windows are all handled the same way. The kernel checks every handle against the process's rights, and closes everything a process left open when it exits. ```cpp #include #include int main() { std::cout << "This process has id " << GetCurrentProcessId() << '\n'; std::cout << "Its main thread has id " << GetCurrentThreadId() << '\n'; return 0; } ``` ```varies This process has id 18324 Its main thread has id 20916 ``` Run it twice and the numbers change: every run is a new process with a new id. Open **Task Manager → Details** while a program is running and you can find it by this id. ## What this means for low-level work Every topic later in the course is about one of these jobs, seen up close. | OS job | Where the course goes deeper | |---|---| | Loading programs and DLLs | Chapter 4 (DLLs), chapter 9 (the PE format) | | Private virtual memory | Chapter 6 (address spaces, pages, protection) | | Scheduling | Chapter 6 (threads), chapter 8 (debugging threads) | | System calls and the Windows API | Chapter 5, chapter 15 | | Handles and rights | Chapter 5 (handles), chapter 6 (access rights) | > [!note] Rights are a feature, not an obstacle > Much of what the OS does is say no: no, you cannot read that process; no, you cannot load that driver. These rules are what keep a PC stable and keep one bad program from compromising the others. The course works with them, using documented interfaces on programs you write yourself. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Thinking a pointer value is a place in RAM > It is a virtual address, meaningful only inside its own process. The same number in another process leads somewhere else, or nowhere. > [!warning] Assuming your thread runs without interruption > The scheduler can pause it between any two instructions. Code that shares data between threads has to be written for that, as chapter 6 shows. > [!warning] Forgetting that handles must be closed > Windows closes them when the process exits, but a long-running game that opens files or threads in a loop and never closes them will run out. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What is the difference between user mode and kernel mode? - User mode is for programs with a window; kernel mode is for console programs - Kernel mode is a debugging mode that pauses the program + Kernel mode has full control of hardware and memory; user mode is restricted and asks the kernel through system calls - User mode runs on one CPU core; kernel mode can use all of them > Normal programs run in user mode and cannot touch anything outside their own process without a system call. ? What does the Windows loader do when a program starts? - It compiles the program's source code into machine code + It maps the program and its DLLs into a new process, links imports, starts a thread - It copies the program into the CPU's registers and jumps to `main` - It checks the program for viruses and then runs it line by line > Compiling happened long before, at build time. The loader's job is setting up the process so the first instruction can run. ? What is a handle? - The memory address of a kernel object - The name of a file, as a string - A pointer to a function the operating system provides + A small number a process uses to refer to a kernel object it has opened > The kernel checks every use of a handle against the process's rights. It is not an address the program could follow itself. ? Why can one process not simply read another process's variables through a pointer? + Each process has its own address space, so the address means nothing elsewhere - Pointers are encrypted by the operating system - The other process's variables are stored on disk, not in memory > The same pointer value in two processes refers to two different places. Reading another process needs the kernel's help through a system call. ? Two processes print the same pointer value. What does that tell you? - They are sharing that piece of memory + Nothing: each has its own address space - One of them has crashed > Virtual addresses are private to each process. The OS maps them to physical memory separately for each one. ? What is a process? - Another name for an `.exe` file + A running copy of a program, with its own memory and threads - A single function running on the CPU > The `.exe` is the file on disk. Starting it creates a process. Starting it twice creates two processes. ? How big is one page of memory on x64 Windows? - 1,024 bytes + 4,096 bytes (`0x1000`) - 65,536 bytes > 65,536 is the allocation granularity, which chapter 6 explains. A page is 4 KB. ? How does a normal Windows program read a file from disk? - It talks to the disk controller directly + It calls a Windows API function, which makes a system call into the kernel - It reads the disk's memory addresses with a pointer > User-mode code cannot touch hardware. The kernel and its drivers do that on the program's behalf. ```
ideas:
- Run the `GetSystemInfo` example and add a line that prints `info.dwNumberOfProcessors`. Compare it with the number of logical processors Task Manager shows on its Performance tab.
- Run the process id example in Visual Studio with a breakpoint on `return 0;`. While it is paused, find the process in Task Manager's Details tab by its id.
- Start the same program twice at once and confirm the two copies have different ids.

cards.q: What is the difference between user mode and kernel mode?
cards.a:
Kernel mode has full control of hardware and memory; user mode is restricted and asks the kernel through system calls

Normal programs run in user mode and cannot touch anything outside their own process without a system call.

cards.q: What does the Windows loader do when a program starts?
cards.a:
It maps the program and its DLLs into a new process, links imports, starts a thread

Compiling happened long before, at build time. The loader's job is setting up the process so the first instruction can run.

A small number a process uses to refer to a kernel object it has opened

The kernel checks every use of a handle against the process's rights. It is not an address the program could follow itself.

cards.q: Why can one process not simply read another process's variables through a pointer?
cards.a:
Each process has its own address space, so the address means nothing elsewhere

The same pointer value in two processes refers to two different places. Reading another process needs the kernel's help through a system call.

cards.q: Two processes print the same pointer value. What does that tell you?
cards.a:
Nothing: each has its own address space

Virtual addresses are private to each process. The OS maps them to physical memory separately for each one.

A running copy of a program, with its own memory and threads

The `.exe` is the file on disk. Starting it creates a process. Starting it twice creates two processes.

cards.q: How big is one page of memory on x64 Windows?
cards.a:
4,096 bytes (`0x1000`)

65,536 is the allocation granularity, which chapter 6 explains. A page is 4 KB.

cards.q: How does a normal Windows program read a file from disk?
cards.a:
It calls a Windows API function, which makes a system call into the kernel

User-mode code cannot touch hardware. The kernel and its drivers do that on the program's behalf.
